decisions.reason: The abstract directly states 'In CLN1 a non-rhythmic gait is seen around 1-1½ years of age.' This clearly establishes CLN1 disease as having the phenotype of non-rhythmic gait.
The abstract directly states 'Shortly after, postural hypotonia and exaggerated tendon reflexes develop.' The context following the CLN1 discussion clearly associates this with CLN1 disease.

The abstract directly states 'Shortly after, postural hypotonia and exaggerated tendon reflexes develop.' within the CLN1 discussion, clearly establishing exaggerated tendon reflexes as a phenotype of CLN1 disease.

The abstract states 'The disease reaches a burnt-out stage during the third year of age and subsequently the children are almost without voluntary movements.' This is in the CLN1 section and describes loss of voluntary movements as a phenotype of CLN1 disease.

The quote states 'gait phenotype in CLN1 is caused by early involvement of the spinal interneurons followed by impact of the cortex and the cortico-spinal tracts.' This explicitly describes early involvement of spinal interneurons as a mechanism (cause) of CLN1 disease phenotype.

The quote explicitly states that gait phenotype in CLN1 'is caused by early involvement of the spinal interneurons followed by impact of the cortex and the cortico-spinal tracts.' The impact on cortex and cortico-spinal tracts is presented as a causal mechanism.

The quote describes 'early involvement of the cerebellum' as a structural/anatomical change that is associated with CLN2 gait abnormalities. 'Early involvement' of brain regions is a structural pathology, not a mechanism. The abstract treats these as anatomical changes accompanying gait phenotype, not as mechanistic explanations of disease pathogenesis.

Similar to candidate 6, 'early involvement of the cortico-spinal pathways' is described as a structural anatomical change, not as a disease mechanism. The abstract treats these as patho-anatomical correlates of gait phenotype, not as mechanistic explanations.
The abstract directly states 'In CLN3, a reduction in walking speed is present at the age of 7-8 years.' This clearly establishes that CLN3 disease has the phenotype of reduced walking speed.

The quote states 'It occurs simultaneously with a reduction in the white matter microstructure and brain connectivity networks.' This describes a simultaneous/concomitant structural change, not a mechanism of disease. The abstract presents white matter microstructure reduction as a patho-anatomical correlate, not as a mechanism causing the phenotype. This is an anatomical observation, not a mechanistic explanation.

The quote states these occur 'simultaneously,' indicating temporal association rather than mechanistic causation. Reduced brain connectivity networks is presented as a structural/anatomical correlate of the phenotype, not as an underlying mechanism of disease pathogenesis.

The abstract directly states 'Functional impairment of the basal ganglia contributing to a parkinsonian gait phenotype occurs in the mid-teens.' within the CLN3 discussion, clearly establishing parkinsonian gait as a phenotype of CLN3 disease.

The abstract states 'In the late teens and early twenties involvement of the peripheral nerves, neurogenic musculoskeletal atrophy, loss of tendon reflexes and postural control are seen.' within the CLN3 section, clearly listing peripheral nerve involvement as a phenotype of CLN3 disease.
